items.readable_text:
Content:
We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

Content:
For example, consider the following vectors:
[MATH: [1; 2; 1]]
How can we find the orthogonal projection [MATH: \mathbf{x}_S] of the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace [MATH: S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?] Notice that since [MATH: \mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,] the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{a}_2] are not orthogonal.

Content:
As usual, we would like to write [MATH: \mathbf{x}] as
[MATH: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},]
where [MATH: \mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/647ee475350f13f6aab009bcc20a387d]

Content:
So, we have
[MATH: x_{S^{⊥}}|= x − x_{S}; = x − (k_{1}a_{1} + k_{2}a_{2}); = x − k_{1}a_{1} − k_{2}a_{2}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,] that is, [MATH: \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,] we obtain
[MATH: {x_{S^{⊥}}⊥a_{1}; x_{S^{⊥}}⊥a_{2}⟹{x_{S^{⊥}} ⋅ a_{1} = 0; x_{S^{⊥}} ⋅ a_{2} = 0.]
Now, we substitute the expression for [MATH: \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}] into the system to get
[MATH: {(x − k_{1}a_{1} − k_{2}a_{2}) ⋅ a_{1} = 0; (x − k_{1}a_{1} − k_{2}a_{2}) ⋅ a_{2} = 0]

Content:
We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
[MATH: [− a_{1} −; − a_{2} −]]

Content:
If we denote
[MATH: [|||; a_{1}|a_{2};|||]]
and [MATH: [k_{1}; k_{2}]] then we obtain
[MATH: A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: proj_{S}x|= Ak; = A(A^{T}A)^{− 1}A^{T}x.]
This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Content:
Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get
[MATH: proj_{S}x|= [1|1; 2|3; 1|1] ⋅ ([1|2|1; 1|3|1] ⋅ [1|1; 2|3; 1|1])^{− 1} ⋅ [1|2|1; 1|3|1] ⋅ [2; 4; 0]; = [1|1; 2|3; 1|1] ⋅ ([6|8; 8|11])^{− 1} ⋅ [10; 14]; = [1|1; 2|3; 1|1] ⋅ (1)/(2)[11|− 8; − 8|6] ⋅ [10; 14]; = [1|1; 2|3; 1|1] ⋅ [− 1; 2]; = [1; 4; 1].]

Content:
Note: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that [MATH: \mathbf v] and [MATH: \mathbf w] are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix [MATH: A] is given by [MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A\left(A^T\!A\right)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.]

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace [MATH: S=\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\}] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3.] In our case, we have [MATH: [|||; v|w;|||]] Therefore, we get the following projection:

[MATH: proj_{S}x|= [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2] ⋅ ([− 2|− 2|2; − 2|− 2|− 2] ⋅ [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2])^{− 1} ⋅ [− 2|− 2|2; − 2|− 2|− 2] ⋅ [2; 0; 8]; = [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2] ⋅ [12|4; 4|12]^{− 1} ⋅ [12; − 20]; = [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2] ⋅ (1)/(32)[3|− 1; − 1|3] ⋅ [12; − 20]; = [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2] ⋅ (1)/(4)[7; − 9]; = [1; 1; 8]]

sections.normalized_html: Verify whether the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3] are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace spanned by the vectors [MATH: \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \},] where [MATH: [4; 3; 1]]
sections.readable_text:
Verify whether the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3] are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace spanned by the vectors [MATH: \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \},] where
[MATH: [4; 3; 1]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we verify whether [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3] are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

[MATH: M|=[4|1|1; 3|1|2; 1|1|4]|R_{3}↔R_{1}; ∼[1|1|4; 3|1|2; 4|1|1]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 3)R_{1}; R_{3}:=R_{3} + (− 4)R_{1}; ∼[1|1|4; 0|− 2|− 10; 0|− 3|− 15]|R_{3}:=R_{3} + (− (3)/(2))R_{2}; ∼[1|1|4; 0|− 2|− 10; 0|0|0]]

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{a}_2] that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix [MATH: A] is given by [MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.]

In our case, we have [MATH: [|||; a_{1}|a_{2};|||]]

Therefore, we get the following projection:

[MATH: proj_{S}x|= [4|1; 3|1; 1|1] ⋅ ([4|3|1; 1|1|1] ⋅ [4|1; 3|1; 1|1])^{− 1} ⋅ [4|3|1; 1|1|1] ⋅ [5; − 1; 1]; = [4|1; 3|1; 1|1] ⋅ [26|8; 8|3]^{− 1} ⋅ [18; 5]; = [4|1; 3|1; 1|1] ⋅ (1)/(14)[3|− 8; − 8|26] ⋅ [18; 5]; = [4|1; 3|1; 1|1][1; − 1]; = [3; 2; 0]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

Content:
For example, consider the following vectors:
[MATH: [1; 2; 1]]
How can we find the orthogonal projection [MATH: \mathbf{x}_S] of the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace [MATH: S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?] Notice that since [MATH: \mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,] the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{a}_2] are not orthogonal.

Content:
As usual, we would like to write [MATH: \mathbf{x}] as
[MATH: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},]
where [MATH: \mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/647ee475350f13f6aab009bcc20a387d]

Content:
So, we have
[MATH: x_{S^{⊥}}|= x − x_{S}; = x − (k_{1}a_{1} + k_{2}a_{2}); = x − k_{1}a_{1} − k_{2}a_{2}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,] that is, [MATH: \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,] we obtain
[MATH: {x_{S^{⊥}}⊥a_{1}; x_{S^{⊥}}⊥a_{2}⟹{x_{S^{⊥}} ⋅ a_{1} = 0; x_{S^{⊥}} ⋅ a_{2} = 0.]
Now, we substitute the expression for [MATH: \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}] into the system to get
[MATH: {(x − k_{1}a_{1} − k_{2}a_{2}) ⋅ a_{1} = 0; (x − k_{1}a_{1} − k_{2}a_{2}) ⋅ a_{2} = 0]

Content:
We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
[MATH: [− a_{1} −; − a_{2} −]]

Content:
If we denote
[MATH: [|||; a_{1}|a_{2};|||]]
and [MATH: [k_{1}; k_{2}]] then we obtain
[MATH: A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: proj_{S}x|= Ak; = A(A^{T}A)^{− 1}A^{T}x.]
This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Content:
Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get
[MATH: proj_{S}x|= [1|1; 2|3; 1|1] ⋅ ([1|2|1; 1|3|1] ⋅ [1|1; 2|3; 1|1])^{− 1} ⋅ [1|2|1; 1|3|1] ⋅ [2; 4; 0]; = [1|1; 2|3; 1|1] ⋅ ([6|8; 8|11])^{− 1} ⋅ [10; 14]; = [1|1; 2|3; 1|1] ⋅ (1)/(2)[11|− 8; − 8|6] ⋅ [10; 14]; = [1|1; 2|3; 1|1] ⋅ [− 1; 2]; = [1; 4; 1].]

Content:
Note: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The General Formula for the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace

Content:
If [MATH: \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}] is a set of linearly independent vectors, then the orthogonal projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace [MATH: S = \textrm{span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}] is given by
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x},]
where [MATH: A] is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n,] that is,
[MATH: [||||…||; a_{1}|a_{2}|…|a_{n};||||…||]]

Content:
Watch out! The fact that [MATH: \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}] must be linearly independent is important. If the vectors are linearly dependent, we need to find the basis of the span before applying the formula.

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane

Example Prompt:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the plane [MATH: \mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{v}+t\mathbf{w},] where [MATH: s,t\in\mathbb R,] and
[MATH: [− 2; − 2; 2]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that [MATH: \mathbf v] and [MATH: \mathbf w] are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix [MATH: A] is given by
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A\left(A^T\!A\right)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.]

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace [MATH: S=\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\}] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3.] In our case, we have
[MATH: [|||; v|w;|||]]
Therefore, we get the following projection:

[MATH: proj_{S}x|= [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2] ⋅ ([− 2|− 2|2; − 2|− 2|− 2] ⋅ [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2])^{− 1} ⋅ [− 2|− 2|2; − 2|− 2|− 2] ⋅ [2; 0; 8]; = [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2] ⋅ [12|4; 4|12]^{− 1} ⋅ [12; − 20]; = [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2] ⋅ (1)/(32)[3|− 1; − 1|3] ⋅ [12; − 20]; = [− 2|− 2; − 2|− 2; 2|− 2] ⋅ (1)/(4)[7; − 9]; = [1; 1; 8]]

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace

Example Prompt:
Verify whether the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3] are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace spanned by the vectors [MATH: \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \},] where
[MATH: [4; 3; 1]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we verify whether [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3] are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

[MATH: M|=[4|1|1; 3|1|2; 1|1|4]|R_{3}↔R_{1}; ∼[1|1|4; 3|1|2; 4|1|1]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 3)R_{1}; R_{3}:=R_{3} + (− 4)R_{1}; ∼[1|1|4; 0|− 2|− 10; 0|− 3|− 15]|R_{3}:=R_{3} + (− (3)/(2))R_{2}; ∼[1|1|4; 0|− 2|− 10; 0|0|0]]

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{a}_2] that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix [MATH: A] is given by
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.]

In our case, we have
[MATH: [|||; a_{1}|a_{2};|||]]

Therefore, we get the following projection:

[MATH: proj_{S}x|= [4|1; 3|1; 1|1] ⋅ ([4|3|1; 1|1|1] ⋅ [4|1; 3|1; 1|1])^{− 1} ⋅ [4|3|1; 1|1|1] ⋅ [5; − 1; 1]; = [4|1; 3|1; 1|1] ⋅ [26|8; 8|3]^{− 1} ⋅ [18; 5]; = [4|1; 3|1; 1|1] ⋅ (1)/(14)[3|− 8; − 8|26] ⋅ [18; 5]; = [4|1; 3|1; 1|1][1; − 1]; = [3; 2; 0]]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Some Intuition Behind the Formula

Content:
As we've already seen, the orthogonal projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto the one-dimensional subspace [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] is given by
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}} \, \mathbf{x} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}} \: \mathbf{a}.]
If we suppose that [MATH: \mathbf{a}] denotes the column-vector [MATH: [|; a;|]] then the dot product [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}] is simply [MATH: \mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{a},] and we can write the formula as follows:
[MATH: proj_{a}x|= ((a ⋅ x))/((a ⋅ a))a; = [((a^{T}x))/((a^{T}a))]a; = a[((a^{T}x))/((a^{T}a))]; = a[(a^{T}a)^{− 1}a^{T}x]; = a(a^{T}a)^{− 1}a^{T}x.]

Content:
Now, let's compare the above with the formula that we use when we want to project onto an arbitrary subspace:
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}]
As we can see, they are basically the same thing!
